data.excerpt: Buying your first home in California comes with unique challenges. Here are the mistakes that trip up new buyers most often — and how to steer clear of them.
body: Purchasing a first home in California can feel like learning a new language overnight — appraisals, impounds, points, prequalification versus preapproval. Because home prices across the state tend to run higher than the national average, small missteps early in the process can have outsized effects on a buyer's budget and timeline. Understanding where first-time buyers commonly stumble is one of the best ways to approach the journey with more clarity and less stress.

One of the most frequent mistakes is assuming that a mortgage prequalification and a mortgage preapproval are the same thing. A prequalification is typically a quick, informal estimate based on self-reported information, while a preapproval usually involves a lender reviewing documentation such as income, assets, and credit history in more depth. Treating a prequalification as a guarantee of financing can lead to disappointment later if numbers don't hold up once verified. Buyers benefit from learning the difference early so they know what stage they're really in before making offers.

Another common pitfall is focusing solely on the interest rate while ignoring the full cost of homeownership. Property taxes, homeowners insurance, mortgage insurance, HOA dues, and maintenance costs can all add up, especially in higher-cost California markets. Rates vary by lender, loan type, and borrower profile, so comparing offers purely on an advertised rate without considering fees, points, and total monthly payment can create a misleading picture. A more complete comparison looks at the full loan estimate, not just the headline number.

Many first-time buyers also make major financial changes right before or during the loan process — opening new credit cards, financing a car, or switching jobs. Lenders typically re-verify credit and employment close to closing, and sudden changes can affect debt-to-income calculations or delay funding altogether. Keeping finances as stable and predictable as possible between application and closing is a simple habit that can prevent unnecessary setbacks.

It's also easy to overlook California-specific programs and assistance options designed to help first-time buyers with down payments or closing costs. Some state and local programs offer deferred-payment or low-interest down payment assistance, though eligibility rules, income limits, and funding availability can change and are not guaranteed to be available at any given time. Rather than assuming these options don't apply, it's worth researching current programs and discussing eligibility with a qualified mortgage professional before ruling anything out.

Finally, many buyers underestimate how important it is to shop around and ask questions. Mortgage terms, fees, and program options can differ significantly between lenders, and relying on a single quote without comparison may mean missing a better-fitting option. Taking time to understand loan types — such as conventional, FHA, or VA financing — and how each might align with a buyer's goals can make the entire process feel less overwhelming. Education, patience, and preparation are often the biggest differentiators between a smooth home purchase and a stressful one. Mettkey exists to help Californians build that foundational understanding, offering plain-language resources so buyers can walk into conversations with lenders feeling informed rather than guessing. First-time home buyers in California often encounter the same avoidable pitfalls — and understanding them early can lead to a smoother, more confident process. A few common patterns worth noting:

1. Delaying pre-approval conversations — waiting too long to understand your general borrowing picture can mean missed opportunities in a fast-moving market.
2. Overlooking total cost of ownership — property taxes, Mello-Roos assessments, HOA dues, and insurance can add up quickly in California, beyond just the mortgage payment itself.
3. Not exploring the full range of loan programs — options like FHA, VA, and CalHFA down payment assistance programs exist, but eligibility and terms vary widely by borrower and lender.
4. Making emotional decisions under market pressure — waiving inspections or contingencies without fully understanding the risk can lead to costly surprises later.

Every borrower's situation is different, and rates, terms, and approval outcomes vary by lender and individual financial profile. There's no one-size-fits-all answer — which is exactly why education matters before you start the buying process.

data.preheader: A quick educational guide to common first-time buyer pitfalls in California's housing market.
data.bodyHtml:
First-Time Home Buyer Mistakes to Avoid in California

Buying your first home in California comes with unique challenges — high prices, competitive markets, and a wide range of loan programs to understand. Whether you're just starting to research or getting ready to talk with lenders, knowing these common mistakes ahead of time may help you feel more prepared.

1. Not Reviewing Credit Early

Many first-time buyers wait until they're ready to apply to check their credit report. Reviewing your credit months in advance gives you time to spot errors or understand how your credit profile may affect the loan programs available to you. Keep in mind that qualification requirements and terms vary by lender and borrower.

2. Focusing Only on the Interest Rate

It's natural to want the lowest possible rate, but rates are only one part of the picture. Loan terms, fees, closing costs, and the type of loan program can all affect the overall cost of a mortgage. Rates and terms vary by lender, loan type, and individual financial circumstances, so it helps to look at the full picture rather than a single number.

3. Not Budgeting for California-Specific Costs

California homeownership often includes costs beyond the mortgage payment, such as property taxes, homeowners insurance (including wildfire-related considerations in some areas), and HOA dues where applicable. Understanding these potential costs early can help you build a more realistic budget.

4. Making Big Financial Changes Mid-Process

Opening new credit accounts, changing jobs, or making large purchases while working through the home buying process can affect how a lender evaluates your application. Many educational resources recommend keeping your financial situation as stable as possible until after closing.

5. Skipping the Education on Loan Programs

California buyers may have access to various loan programs — conventional, FHA, VA, or state-specific assistance programs like CalHFA — each with different requirements. Learning about these options in advance can help you ask better questions when you do speak with a lender or broker.

6. Not Planning for Closing Costs and Reserves

Some buyers focus entirely on the down payment and forget that closing costs and cash reserves may also be needed. Typical programs may include different requirements for reserves, so it's worth researching this early rather than being surprised later.

7. Not Comparing Multiple Lenders

Loan offers, fees, and communication styles can vary significantly between lenders. Taking time to understand how to compare offers — rather than accepting the first one presented — is a skill that can serve you throughout the home buying process.

Keep Learning Before You Buy

data.hook: Myth: You need 20% down to buy a home in California.
data.body: Many first-time buyers assume a 20% down payment is required, but conventional loans can go as low as 3% down and FHA programs as low as 3.5%, with some VA and USDA options requiring none for eligible borrowers. Putting down less typically means paying mortgage insurance and may affect the interest rate offered, so the trade-offs matter and vary by lender and borrower profile. California also has state and local down payment assistance programs that buyers can research independently. Educational purposes only. Mettkey is not a lender or broker. NMLS #2779492 | Shiva T. Mettke.

data.hook: Myth: A high debt-to-income ratio automatically disqualifies you.
data.body: Lenders often cap DTI around 43-50%, but 'strong' compensating factors — like higher credit scores, larger reserves, or a bigger down payment — can allow some borrowers to qualify above those typical thresholds. DTI guidelines differ by loan program (FHA, VA, conventional) and by individual lender overlays, so there's no single universal cutoff. This means a borrower who assumes they're automatically out of the running may still have options worth exploring with a licensed loan professional. Educational purposes only. Mettkey is not a lender or broker. NMLS #2779492 | Shiva T. Mettke.

data.hook: Myth: Renting is always 'throwing money away' compared to buying.
data.body: In high-cost California markets, the math isn't automatic — closing costs, property taxes, maintenance, and opportunity cost on a down payment can outweigh the benefits of buying if you plan to move within a few years. Renting also isn't 'wasted' money; it buys flexibility and avoids exposure to home price swings or large repair bills. Whether buying makes sense depends on local price-to-rent ratios, how long you plan to stay, and your personal financial situation, not a blanket rule. Educational purposes only.
